subtopics.title: Monopoly — One Seller, and the Price Maker's Diagram

questions.question: Which combination correctly defines a monopoly?
options: One seller, a product with no close substitutes, blocked entry
Many sellers of identical products with free entry
A few large sellers watching each other's prices
Many sellers of differentiated products

questions.question: A monopolist sells 20 units at R50, or 21 units at R49. What is the marginal revenue of the 21st unit?
After finding output where MR = MC, where does the monopolist's PRICE come from?
options: The MR curve at that output
The minimum of the AC curve
The demand curve, vertically above that output
The intersection of MC and AC

questions.question: Why can a monopolist's economic profit persist into the long run?
options: Because its costs always fall over time
Because consumers prefer monopolies
Because the government guarantees its revenue
Because blocked entry prevents new competitors from eroding the profit

subtopics.title: Oligopoly — the Few, the Kink, and the Cartel Temptation

questions.question: The defining feature of oligopoly is ...
options: mutual interdependence — each firm's best move depends on its rivals' reactions
a single seller with blocked entry
perfectly informed buyers
government ownership of the largest firm

questions.question: In the kinked demand curve model, why is the curve elastic ABOVE the kink?
options: Because rivals always match a price increase
Because a firm that raises its price alone loses many customers to rivals who hold still
Because demand is fixed by regulation
Because costs rise with output

questions.question: Since price wars are self-defeating, oligopolists typically compete through ...
options: continuous deep price cutting
refusing to advertise
non-price competition: branding, advertising, loyalty schemes, service and features
leaving the market

questions.question: Why are cartels described as inherently unstable?
options: Because they are always profitable for every member
Because governments usually subsidise them
Because consumers organise boycotts against them
Because each member gains by secretly undercutting the agreed price, which unravels the pact

subtopics.title: Monopolistic Competition — Many Sellers, Each Slightly Special

questions.question: Which features define monopolistic competition?
options: Many sellers, differentiated products, free entry and exit
One seller, unique product, blocked entry
Few sellers, homogeneous product, difficult entry
Many sellers, identical products, perfect knowledge

questions.question: Why does a monopolistically competitive firm face a gently downward-sloping demand curve?
options: Because it is the only seller in the market
Because product differentiation creates some customer loyalty, while close substitutes limit its price power
Because the government fixes a price band
Because its costs slope downward

questions.question: What eliminates economic profit in this structure in the long run?
options: Government price controls
Rising wage costs
Free entry — newcomers shave away customers until the demand curve is tangent to AC
Consumers losing interest in variety

questions.question: "Excess capacity" at the long-run tangency means the firm ...
options: produces more than the profit-maximising output
operates at the minimum of its AC curve
earns persistent economic profit
produces less than the output that would minimise its average cost

subtopics.title: The Four Structures Side by Side

questions.question: Rank the structures by number of sellers, from most to fewest.
options: Perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly
Monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition
Oligopoly, monopoly, perfect competition, monopolistic competition
Monopolistic competition, monopoly, oligopoly, perfect competition

questions.question: Which structure faces a KINKED demand curve at the ruling price?
options: Monopoly
Oligopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition

questions.question: Which structure delivers BOTH allocative and productive efficiency in the long run?
options: Monopoly
Oligopoly
Perfect competition only
Monopolistic competition

questions.question: The two "dials" that generate all four market structures are ...
options: advertising budget and firm size
tax rate and interest rate
wage level and technology
the slope of the firm's demand curve and the ease of entry

subtopics.title: The Only Ferry Across the Lagoon

questions.question: Unlike the butternut seller, the ferry company can set its own fare because ...
options: it faces no close substitute — passengers have no identical rival to switch to
ferry tickets are cheaper than butternuts
the government sets ferry fares
passengers never respond to prices

questions.question: What limits the ferry's fare even though it is a monopoly?
options: The Competition Commission sets a maximum fare
The demand curve — at high fares, passengers drive around, share lifts or stay home
The company's sense of fairness
Rival ferries on the same lagoon

questions.question: Cutting the fare from R30 to R28 to attract new passengers costs the ferry invisibly because ...
options: fuel costs rise with each new passenger
new passengers pay less tax
everyone already aboard also pays the lower fare, eating into the gain
the harbour charges more at lower fares

questions.question: When one ferry can carry the whole town more cheaply than two could, the sensible policy is ...
options: forcing a second ferry to launch
banning the ferry service
letting the ferry charge whatever it likes
accepting the natural monopoly but regulating its fares

subtopics.title: Three Bakeries and a Staring Contest

questions.question: Why does no bakery raise its bread price alone?
options: Rivals will hold their prices and its customers will switch suppliers
The law forbids price increases
Higher prices always reduce costs
The other bakeries would immediately raise prices too

questions.question: Why does cutting the price also fail as a strategy?
options: Customers distrust cheaper bread
Rivals match the cut, leaving all three selling at less to the same customers
Cutting prices is illegal collusion
The bakery's costs fall with the price

questions.question: The bakeries' fresher deliveries, sponsor boards and new loaf varieties are examples of ...
options: predatory pricing
price leadership
non-price competition
market division

questions.question: If the three owners agree to raise prices together, which forces eventually break the pact?
options: Rising flour prices and load shedding
Customer loyalty and better service
New bread recipes and advertising
Secret cheating by members and prosecution under the Competition Act

questions.question: Each takeaway can charge slightly more than its neighbours because ...
options: differentiation — regulars value its particular chips, hours or service and tolerate a small premium
the rank committee assigns each shop its price
food prices are fixed by law
customers cannot see other takeaways

questions.question: What happens when one takeaway starts earning fat margins on this street?
options: The margins grow forever
New takeaways open nearby and shave its customers away until profit returns to normal
The other shops must close by law
Customers stop buying chips

questions.question: The half-idle fryers in the mid-afternoon lull illustrate ...
options: allocative efficiency
economies of scale
excess capacity — the standing cost of a differentiated street
predatory pricing

questions.question: What do consumers receive in exchange for the street's slight inefficiency?
options: Lower prices than perfect competition would deliver
Guaranteed quality standards
Persistent economic profits
Variety — a range of genuinely different products and services to choose from
